subtopics.title: Subsidence, Convergence and the Rain Switch

questions.question: Converging surface winds produce rain because:
options: Air piling in from the sides can only escape upward, and rising air cools adiabatically until its vapour condenses into cloud
Converging winds compress the air and warm it
Convergence pushes moisture underground
Converging winds cancel each other out, leaving calm dry air

questions.question: Subsiding air makes rain nearly impossible because:
options: Sinking air collects moisture from the clouds it passes
Descent compresses and warms the air, collapsing its relative humidity and dissolving cloud, while divergence spreads it outward at the surface
Sinking air is always saturated
Subsidence only happens at night

questions.question: A temperature inversion acts as a ceiling because:
options: Cold air above sucks the thermals upward
The inversion layer physically blocks sunlight
A rising bubble of surface air reaches the layer where temperature climbs with height, finds itself cooler and heavier than its surroundings, and stops
Inversions only form over oceans

questions.question: Africa's permanently wet and permanently dry belts sit respectively:
options: At the poles and the equator
At 60 degrees and at the equator
Along both coasts and across the interior
Under the equatorial convergence, and under the subsiding subtropical highs near 30 degrees north and south

subtopics.title: The ITCZ — the Rain Belt That Migrates

questions.question: The ITCZ is defined as:
options: The low-pressure trough where the south-east trades of the southern hemisphere meet the north-east trades of the northern hemisphere, forcing air upward on a grand scale
The boundary between the westerlies and the polar easterlies
A line of permanent high pressure over the equator
The track followed by mid-latitude cyclones

questions.question: In January the ITCZ lies:
options: Over the Sahel at about 15 to 20 degrees north
Across southern Africa — over Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe, brushing South Africa's far north — driving the southern summer rains
Exactly on the equator all month
Over the Mediterranean

questions.question: The Congo Basin records a double rainfall maximum because:
options: Two oceans supply it with moisture
It has two wet oceansides
The ITCZ crosses it twice a year — once travelling north and once travelling south
The subtropical highs visit it twice a year

questions.question: Zimbabwe and the Sahel are vulnerable to drought in a way the Congo Basin is not because:
options: They have no rivers
Their soils cannot absorb rain
They lie under permanent subsidence
They sit near the limits of the ITCZ's journey, so a season in which the belt stalls or arrives weakly leaves them with little or no rain

subtopics.title: The Kalahari High and the Oceans on Either Side

questions.question: In winter the interior plateau stays dry because:
options: The strong Kalahari High drives an inversion that lies below the escarpment crest, so moist maritime air cannot climb onto the plateau
The Kalahari High disappears completely
The ITCZ sits over Gauteng
The oceans freeze along both coasts

questions.question: Summer thunderstorms return to the plateau because:
options: The escarpment is lower in summer
Surface heating weakens the high and lifts the inversion above the escarpment, letting Indian Ocean moisture pour over the eastern rim
The Benguela Current warms up in summer
Cold fronts cross the plateau daily in summer

questions.question: Air resting on the cold Benguela Current becomes:
options: Warm, moist and unstable
Warm and dry
Cool, dry and stable — able to deliver fog to the shore but almost never rain
Saturated and stormy

questions.question: Richards Bay is green and humid while Alexander Bay, at nearly the same latitude, is desert because:
options: Richards Bay receives frontal rain all year
Alexander Bay lies at much higher altitude
The two towns lie in different hemispheres
The warm Mozambique-Agulhas water makes east-coast air moist and unstable, while the cold Benguela keeps west-coast air dry and stable — opposite currents, opposite climates

subtopics.title: Synoptic Charts, Satellites and El Niño

questions.question: On a synoptic chart, a closed cell labelled H with widely spaced isobars promises:
options: Subsiding air, settled clear weather and light winds
Rising air and heavy rain
Gale-force winds
An approaching cold front

questions.question: A cold front is drawn on the chart as:
options: A double dashed line along the equator
A line of triangles pointing in the direction the front is moving, usually approaching the country from the south-west
A circle of tightly packed isobars
A row of semicircles pointing backward

questions.question: In the station model, the wind shaft and its feathers show:
options: The temperature and dew point
Cloud height and type
The direction the wind comes FROM, with each full feather counting ten knots of speed
The direction the wind is blowing toward, with feathers counting rainfall

questions.question: During the 2023-24 El Niño, southern Africa experienced:
options: Record flooding in every province
No change from normal seasons
A doubled maize harvest
A seared midsummer with shrunken rains that cut harvests across Zambia, Zimbabwe and South Africa

subtopics.title: The Duvet and the Hot-Air Balloon

questions.question: In the two pictures, the hot-air balloon and the pressed-down duvet stand for:
options: Convergence with rising air and rain, versus subsidence with sinking air and no rain
Day weather versus night weather
Summer versus winter at the equator
Ocean climates versus desert climates

questions.question: The Sahara, Kalahari and Namib all lie:
options: Under the rising balloon at the equator
Beneath the two duvets — the subsiding subtropical highs near 30 degrees north and south
Along the polar front
In the path of the ITCZ all year

questions.question: Smoke over a plateau town on a winter morning climbing and then flattening out sideways like a table top reveals:
options: A cold front passing overhead
Strong convergence at the surface
The temperature inversion — a warm layer aloft that rising air cannot break through, so the sky stays clear
The arrival of the ITCZ

subtopics.title: The Water Truck on Its Route

questions.question: The water truck in the picture stands for:
options: The ITCZ — the storm band that migrates north and south along the continent chasing the overhead sun, about a month behind it
The Benguela Current
A mid-latitude cold front
The Kalahari High

questions.question: In July the truck is parked:
options: Over Zimbabwe and Angola
At the northern end of its route, watering the Sahel, while southern Africa waits dry in winter sunshine
Over the Western Cape
At the South Pole end of the route

questions.question: Houses at the middle of the route get watered twice a year, and houses near the ends only once, which corresponds to:
options: Winter rainfall on the coasts and summer rainfall inland
Fog on the west coast and rain on the east coast
A double rainfall maximum near the equator and a single summer maximum near the tropics
Two dry seasons at the equator

questions.question: Most tropical droughts are described as 'a truck that never quite arrived' because:
options: Water trucks cannot cross the equator
Droughts are caused by too much convergence
The trade winds stop blowing entirely in drought years
Places near the limits of the ITCZ's journey lose their whole rainy season when the belt stalls short or turns back early

subtopics.title: Two Pots and the Weather Map

questions.question: In the two-pot picture, the simmering pot and the iced pot are:
options: The warm Mozambique-Agulhas water feeding moist rising air on the east coast, and the cold Benguela keeping west-coast air dry, stable and foggy
Summer and winter over the plateau
The equatorial low and the polar high
Two stages of the water cycle

questions.question: The security gate on the escarpment describes:
options: The berg wind blowing down to the coast
The Kalahari High's inversion — bolted below the rim in winter to lock moisture out, lifted above the rim in summer to let it flood in
A line of cold fronts queuing offshore
The jet stream crossing the plateau

questions.question: Reading a station on the chart, the two numbers at upper left and lower left are:
options: Wind speed and rainfall
Pressure and visibility
Air temperature above dew-point temperature — and the closer they sit, the moister the air
Maximum and minimum temperature for the week

questions.question: Translated into plain language, El Niño and La Niña mean for our summers:
options: Both bring identical weather to southern Africa
El Niño floods the interior; La Niña dries it
Neither affects Africa at all
El Niño — warm Pacific water, usually thinner summer rains; La Niña — cool Pacific water, usually fatter, wetter summers
